question: Why is watching a patient walk (their gait) such an important part of a nursing assessment?

options.A: It replaces the need to check vital signs during an admission
options.B: It measures the exact level of calcium circulating in the blood
options.C: It provides a definitive laboratory diagnosis for osteoporosis
options.D: It reveals hidden balance issues and weaknesses in weight-bearing joints

explanation: A quick look at how someone walks can tell you a lot about their balance and joint strength before they take a nasty fall! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T24#GNS222_U1_T24_h4)

question: What is the main goal of therapeutic phlebotomy in polycythaemia?

options.A: To increase blood pressure
options.B: To remove excess white blood cells
options.C: To provide iron for the liver
options.D: To reduce red blood cell mass and hematocrit

explanation: Phlebotomy is just safely removing some blood to lower the packed cell volume (hematocrit) and thin things out! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h6)

question: Which sign in an enlarged lymph node strongly points toward cancer (malignancy)?

options.A: Soft, tender, and mobile
options.B: Small, rubbery, and painful
options.C: Hard, fixed, and painless
options.D: Warm, pulsating, and soft

explanation: Cancerous lymph nodes are typically firm or hard, stuck tightly in place (fixed), and usually don't hurt when you press them. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the main root cause of inherited degenerative diseases that affect the brain?

options.A: Traumatic head injuries from physical accidents
options.B: Acute bacterial infections of the central nervous system
options.C: Genetic mutations passed down through families
options.D: Severe nutritional deficiencies in early childhood

explanation: You've got this! These conditions happen because of faulty genes passed down in families, which slowly break down brain tissue over time. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h1)

question: What training tool is commonly used to help healthcare providers address personal biases toward abortion patients?

options.A: Mandatory pharmaceutical sales and marketing courses
options.B: Value clarification and attitude transformation workshops
options.C: Strict legal prosecution guidelines for nursing students
options.D: Advanced surgical training in abdominal hysterectomy

explanation: Well done! These workshops help staff examine their own beliefs and separate personal bias from their duty to save lives. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T021#GNS226_U5_T021_h7)

question: What is a major sign of nerve damage in advanced leprosy during a physical check?

options.A: Painful joint swelling and generalized muscle rigidity
options.B: Sudden widespread bruising and petechiae on the skin
options.C: Spastic paralysis with hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.D: Enlarged, tender nerve trunks and sensory loss

explanation: Spot on! The bacteria attack the nerves directly, making them swollen, painful to touch, and causing the skin over them to lose feeling. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h2)

question: What happens to the bladder and urethra during 'urethral hypermobility' when a patient coughs?

options.A: The bladder instantly shrinks in size
options.B: The urethral sphincter locks tightly shut to block flow
options.C: The detrusor muscle contracts with too much force
options.D: The bladder and urethra drop downward due to weak support

explanation: When the pelvic tissues are a bit weak, coughing causes the bladder and urethra to sag downward instead of staying firmly in place. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: Why is internal haemorrhage often harder to detect quickly than external haemorrhage?

options.A: Internal blood vessels do not contain red blood cells
options.B: The blood is hidden inside body cavities and tissues
options.C: Internal bleeding stops automatically without any medical help
options.D: The body instantly absorbs all escaped internal blood

explanation: Because the bleeding occurs within closed body spaces like the abdomen or chest, there is no visible sign on the skin surface. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h1)

question: Why do family members often feel so distressed when a dying patient stops eating?

options.A: They are worried about the cost of purchasing groceries
options.B: They know that eating is the only cure for their illness
options.C: They believe the hospital kitchen is refusing to cook
options.D: They may view food as a symbol of care and worry the patient is being neglected

explanation: Very true. In our cultures, feeding someone is a deep act of love, so seeing them refuse food can feel heartbreaking to the family. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h5)

question: Why can a patient with a chronic illness still be placed toward the high-wellness end of the continuum?

options.A: Chronic illnesses automatically cure themselves over time
options.B: Medical tests cannot detect chronic conditions on the continuum
options.C: A chronic diagnosis means the disease has completely gone away
options.D: They can achieve a good quality of life and manage their symptoms well

explanation: Wellness involves mental and social well-being alongside physical status, allowing people with chronic conditions to feel well. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h1)

question: Who should be cared for using standard precautions in a hospital?

options.A: Every patient, regardless of their diagnosis
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Only patients with confirmed viral infections
options.D: Only individuals coughing or showing rashes

explanation: Standard precautions are universal and must be applied to all patients because infection status is not always known upfront. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h4)

question: What do blood disorders primarily affect?

options.A: Chronic electrical malfunctions of the heart muscle
options.B: Primary infections of the digestive tract lining
options.C: Conditions affecting blood components and plasma
options.D: Abnormalities restricted only to bone structure

explanation: Blood disorders are all about our blood cells, platelets, and plasma. You've got this! Think of them as troubles within our body's transport system. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T13#GNS311_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why are electrolytes important for the body?

options.A: They act as the main source of daily energy
options.B: They help run nerve signals and muscle contractions
options.C: They store extra fat inside the tissues
options.D: They prevent the body from ever losing water

explanation: Electrolytes carry electrical charges that allow nerves to fire and muscles, including the heart, to contract properly. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T7#GNS123_U3_T7_h1)

question: What is an important step when preparing a conscious patient for suctioning?

options.A: Explaining what will happen to reduce anxiety and fear
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill before starting
options.C: Telling them not to cough under any circumstances
options.D: Asking them to hold their breath until the procedure ends

explanation: Clear communication helps calm the patient, ensuring better cooperation and less panic during a vulnerable moment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: How would you best describe peristalsis?

options.A: Wave-like muscle contractions that push food forward
options.B: Localized churning that mixes food in the small intestine
options.C: The absorption of water through the large bowel wall
options.D: The secretion of digestive enzymes by the pancreas

explanation: Spot on! Think of peristalsis like a wave of muscle squeezes moving food steadily along down the digestive tube. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is a major sign of a high bowel blockage like a duodenal obstruction?

options.A: Inability to pass flatus
options.B: Bright red rectal bleeding
options.C: Frequent projectile vomiting
options.D: Watery diarrhea with mucus

explanation: Spot on! When the upper digestive tract is blocked, food and fluids have nowhere to go but back up, leading to frequent vomiting of stomach contents. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T7#GNS213_U3_T7_h3)

question: Why is fast teamwork among healthcare staff so essential when managing GI complications?

options.A: Conditions can deteriorate into life-threatening emergencies very quickly
options.B: Nurses are not allowed to touch patients without a doctor present
options.C: Medical staff must share paperwork equally among themselves
options.D: Collaborative care guarantees that surgery will never be needed

explanation: You got it! Emergencies like bowel tears or massive bleeding move fast, meaning the team has to act together instantly to keep the patient safe. Teamwork makes the dream work in nursing! [learn more](GNS213_U3_T14#GNS213_U3_T14_h8)

question: Which laboratory test is used to definitively diagnose sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: Coagulation profile test
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Haemoglobin electrophoresis

explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the gold standard test! It separates different types of haemoglobin in a sample so the lab can clearly spot abnormal haemoglobin S. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which implanted device is an absolute contraindication for an MRI scan?

options.A: Permanent dental fillings
options.B: Titanium total hip replacements
options.C: Certain older cardiac pacemakers
options.D: Plastic heart valve repairs

explanation: The strong magnet can interfere with the electrical wiring of older pacemakers, making them dangerous for the patient. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T12#GNS123_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why is suction applied intermittently rather than continuously during airway clearance?

options.A: To allow the suction machine time to build up mechanical pressure
options.B: To make sure the sterile catheter stays clean on the inside
options.C: To prevent severe damage to the airway lining and low oxygen levels
options.D: To give the nurse enough time to measure the suction gauge

explanation: Continuous suctioning pulls too much air out of the lungs and aggressively grips the delicate tissue inside the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: What is the main reason we practice standard precautions in everyday nursing?

options.A: To prevent the transmission of infections between patients and staff
options.B: To ensure medications dissolve faster in the patient's bloodstream
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital cleaning supplies
options.D: To eliminate the need for documenting medication administration

explanation: Standard precautions are your trusty shield! They keep both you and your patients safe from passing germs back and forth during care. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is 'intermittent claudication' in patients with blocked leg arteries?

options.A: Sudden chest pain that happens only when sleeping
options.B: Swelling and redness in the ankles at the end of the day
options.C: Numbness in the fingers when exposed to cold
options.D: Muscle cramping in the legs triggered by walking and eased by rest

explanation: When leg arteries are narrowed, walking starves the muscles of oxygen, causing cramps. Once the patient rests, the pain goes away! That predictable pattern is claudication. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why must you check IV lines and power cords before adjusting a smart bed's position?

options.A: To prevent lines from becoming pinched or disconnected during articulation
options.B: To ensure the bed connects properly to the central hospital Wi-Fi
options.C: To prevent the bed's built-in scale from registering incorrect weights
options.D: To keep the floor clear so housekeeping can mop underneath

explanation: As the bed moves up or down, it can easily pull or snap tight IV lines and oxygen tubing if you haven't checked them first. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T7#GNS212_U4_T7_h5)

question: What actually is 'cor pulmonale'?

options.A: Bleeding into the chest cavity following trauma
options.B: An infection of the lining surrounding the lungs
options.C: Right-sided heart failure caused by long-term lung disease
options.D: A sudden collapse of a lung lobe due to a blocked airway

explanation: You nailed it. Long-term lung trouble makes the heart work extra hard on the right side, eventually leading to right-sided heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h3)

question: What is the main reason a patient with acute pancreatitis is kept NPO (nothing by mouth)?

options.A: To rest the pancreas and stop the release of digestive enzymes
options.B: To prevent choking during sudden episodes of severe vomiting
options.C: To keep the bowel completely clean for diagnostic X-rays
options.D: To prepare the stomach for emergency surgical removal

explanation: Brilliant! Keeping the patient NPO means no food enters the gut, which gives the hardworking pancreas a well-deserved break so it stops producing damaging enzymes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: A client gets mild sedation to stay calm during a long MRI. What must the nurse watch most closely?

options.A: Breathing rate and oxygen levels
options.B: Bowel sounds in all four abdominal areas
options.C: The exact room temperature
options.D: How fast the client can walk afterward

explanation: Sedatives can slow down breathing, so keeping an eye on the patient's respiratory rate and oxygen is top priority! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T8#GNS222_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is the medical name for nearsightedness?

options.A: Hyperopia
options.B: Myopia
options.C: Presbyopia
options.D: Astigmatism

explanation: Myopia means you can see things close up clearly, but far-away objects look blurry because light focuses just short of the retina. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h2)

question: Why do nurses worry so much about secondary complications after a bone fracture?

options.A: They only affect the skin layers surrounding the bone injury.
options.B: They can sometimes become more dangerous than the original break.
options.C: They always require immediate amputation of the affected limb.
options.D: They prevent the patient from ever walking without crutches.

explanation: While a broken bone hurts badly, issues that happen afterwards—like severe infections or blood clots—can actually threaten a patient's life or limb. Spotting them early is a key part of your nursing care! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T23#GNS222_U1_T23_h1)

question: What is the gold-standard test to confirm a patient truly has gout?

options.A: Performing a standard chest X-ray on the patient
options.B: Measuring the daily protein intake in the diet
options.C: Checking a routine blood pressure reading in the clinic
options.D: Examining joint fluid under a microscope for crystals

explanation: You got it! Drawing a little fluid out of the angry joint and spotting those sneaky uric acid crystals under a microscope gives a 100% definite diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T16#GNS222_U1_T16_h5)

question: A patient is scheduled for an upper GI scope to check ongoing internal bleeding. What is the main goal?

options.A: To permanently widen the upper stomach muscle walls
options.B: To flush out the entire digestive tract with sterile water
options.C: To identify the exact source of bleeding and treat it if possible
options.D: To replace damaged stomach lining with synthetic tissue

explanation: Spot on! The camera helps find where the blood is coming from, and doctors can often use tiny tools through the scope to stop it right away. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T2#GNS221_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the main difference between clinical fear and general worry?

options.A: It cannot be managed by nursing interventions.
options.B: It is a response to an immediate, identifiable threat.
options.C: It is completely unrelated to physical safety.
options.D: It only occurs after a surgical operation is finished.

explanation: Spot on! Fear pops up when there is a specific, right-in-front-of-you danger, whereas worry tends to be a bit more vague and unfocused. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T11#GNS123_U3_T11_h1)

question: Why do doctors prescribe the steroid dexamethasone to hospitalized COVID-19 patients?

options.A: To dissolve existing blood clots in the lower legs
options.B: To stimulate the appetite and prevent severe weight loss
options.C: To suppress severe and damaging body inflammation
options.D: To kill the coronavirus directly inside the lungs

explanation: Correct! Dexamethasone helps calm down that over-enthusiastic immune response that wreaks havoc on the lungs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why shouldn't you try to push a protruding bone back under the skin during emergency care?

options.A: It can damage surrounding blood vessels and nerves and introduce deep infection.
options.B: It causes immediate paralysis of the entire central nervous system.
options.C: It makes it impossible for the doctor to take a clear X-ray later.
options.D: It automatically guarantees that the bone will never heal properly.

explanation: Pushing it back in can accidentally slice major blood vessels or nerves, and drag surface germs deep inside the sterile bone. Always leave bone repositioning to the medical team! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T4#GNS112_U7_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of using the surgical safety checklist in the operating room?

options.A: To evaluate the clinical performance of junior medical students
options.B: To prevent wrong-site surgery and reduce preventable surgical errors
options.C: To speed up the turnover time between consecutive surgical cases
options.D: To ensure the hospital insurance policy covers the surgical fees

explanation: Communication saves lives! The checklist keeps everyone on the same page so mistakes are caught before they happen. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T4#GNS123_U5_T4_h5)

question: How does a rehabilitation nurse act as a bridge for the healthcare team around the clock?

options.A: By writing the medical diagnoses for the attending physician
options.B: By carrying daytime therapy goals into everyday 24-hour ward routines
options.C: By replacing the medical social worker during discharge meetings
options.D: By performing all physical and occupational therapy exercises alone

explanation: Nurses are at the bedside 24/7! We help make sure the skills patients learn during short therapy sessions are practiced all day long on the ward. [learn more](GNS123_U6_T3#GNS123_U6_T3_h2)

question: When a nurse asks a patient, 'What makes your stomach pain better or worse?', what are they checking?

options.A: Severity and duration
options.B: Quality and onset
options.C: Provoking and palliating factors
options.D: Region and radiation

explanation: Spot on! Asking what triggers or relieves the discomfort helps you figure out the provoking (starting) and palliating (soothing) factors. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h3)

question: Why is it dangerous to keep expired medication anywhere near active stock supplies?

options.A: It creates a high risk of accidentally administering degraded drugs to a patient
options.B: It automatically invalidates the expiry dates of neighboring boxes
options.C: It takes up space that should be used for cleaning supplies
options.D: It causes the electric lights in the storage room to flicker

explanation: Closeness to active stock increases the chance that a busy nurse will grab an expired item during an emergency. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T19#GNS122_U3_T19_h7)

question: A client with rheumatoid arthritis wakes up with severe joint stiffness that lasts for nearly two hours. What does this tell you as a nurse?

options.A: It represents normal muscle fatigue from daily exercise
options.B: It indicates active and ongoing systemic inflammation
options.C: It suggests the client is experiencing a sudden bone fracture
options.D: It points to a localized soft tissue injury from a fall

explanation: Morning stiffness that drags on for an hour or more is a major red flag for active inflammation inside the joints. Great nursing assessment catches this early! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T11#GNS222_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why is washing out the stomach (gastric lavage) rarely recommended nowadays for routine poisoning cases?

options.A: Lavage only works if the patient drank pure alcohol or petroleum products.
options.B: Activated charcoal completely replaces the need for any physical stomach cleaning.
options.C: The procedure carries significant risks of aspiration and mechanical injury to the esophagus.
options.D: Stomach contents empty into the small intestine within seconds of swallowing.

explanation: Passing a thick tube down into the stomach can easily cause bleeding, injury, or worse—pushing the poison into the lungs. That's why we rely on safer methods now! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T5#GNS112_U7_T5_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal symptom of the postpartum blues?

options.A: Temporary fatigue from broken sleep patterns
options.B: Mild mood swings and unexpected crying spells
options.C: Severe delusions and thoughts of harming the infant
options.D: Feeling slightly overwhelmed by new responsibilities

explanation: Crying spells and feeling overwhelmed are totally normal as hormones shift. However, delusions or thoughts of hurting the baby are never normal blues—they are signs of a severe emergency like postpartum psychosis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h6)

question: A patient with hearing loss is struggling to catch your discharge instructions. What should you do first?

options.A: Ask a family member to take over all patient care responsibilities
options.B: Face the patient directly and speak in a clear, moderate tone
options.C: Shout loudly from across the room so they can hear better
options.D: Stop talking and write everything down in complex medical terms

explanation: Spot on! Facing them lets them see your face and lip-read, which makes understanding much easier. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T3#GNS112_U3_T3_h6)

question: What causes skin to become thick, rough, and leathery, a condition we call lichenification?

options.A: A sudden bacterial infection inside a hair follicle
options.B: Rapid accumulation of watery fluid underneath a bulla
options.C: Chronic scratching and rubbing over a long period
options.D: Exposure to intense ultraviolet sunlight without protection

explanation: When a patient keeps scratching the same spot over and over, the skin fights back by getting thick and leathery. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h3)

question: What causes crackles (rales) to be heard during lung auscultation?

options.A: Fluid or secretions popping open collapsed alveoli
options.B: Air rushing through severely narrowed large bronchi
options.C: Air trapped in the upper respiratory tract
options.D: Inflamed pleural membranes rubbing against each other

explanation: Crackles occur when moisture or fluid causes tiny air sacs to snap open during inspiration. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h4)

question: How does long-term fear and stress affect a patient's physical healing?

options.A: It speeds up tissue repair and lowers blood glucose.
options.B: It has no measurable impact on physical recovery.
options.C: It impairs wound healing and suppresses the immune system.
options.D: It completely stops the need for pain medication.

explanation: You're correct! High stress hormones like cortisol hang around during prolonged fear, which slows down tissue repair and weakens immunity. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T11#GNS123_U3_T11_h7)

question: Why is proper body alignment especially critical for an immobile patient?

options.A: Bones become completely rigid and cannot be moved after one hour
options.B: Immobile patients require less blood flow to their limbs
options.C: Natural body weight causes joints to twist into abnormal postures without support
options.D: Immobile patients cannot feel pain in their joints

explanation: Without active movement, gravity pulls limbs into awkward positions that can hurt joints and nerves. Pillows and rolls are your best friends here! [learn more](GNS112_U4_T8#GNS112_U4_T8_h1)

question: What is the main goal of an endocrine suppression test?

options.A: To measure how fast the kidneys reabsorb glucose from the urine
options.B: To see if a gland stops producing hormones when given a suppressing agent
options.C: To stimulate a sleeping gland into producing maximum hormone levels
options.D: To permanently destroy overactive cells inside the adrenal cortex

explanation: Exactly! While stimulation tests wake glands up, suppression tests check if an overactive gland knows how to quiet down when it's supposed to. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h4)

question: A nurse reviews attendance records and participant feedback after a nutrition workshop. What phase of the nursing process for community programs does this represent?

options.A: Planning
options.B: Evaluation
options.C: Assessment
options.D: Diagnosis

explanation: Reviewing records and gathering feedback after a program is finished is part of evaluating its success. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T2#GNS225_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why is a urinalysis always done when checking for stress incontinence?

options.A: To check kidney function and filtration rates
options.B: To measure the exact amount of residual urine left in the bladder
options.C: To test the patient for diabetes and high blood sugar levels
options.D: To rule out a urinary tract infection that can cause similar symptoms

explanation: Infections can mimic incontinence by irritating the bladder, so checking the urine first helps doctors make a clear diagnosis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: In which layer of the uterus does uterine cancer most commonly start?

options.A: Myometrium
options.B: Perimetrium
options.C: Cervical stroma
options.D: Endometrium

explanation: Spot on! The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus, and that is where most uterine cancers begin. Keep up the great work! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: How would you describe an 'asymptomatic carrier' to a fellow nursing student?

options.A: An individual who is currently experiencing severe symptoms of disease
options.B: A person who carries a pathogen without showing any signs of illness
options.C: A patient who has fully recovered and no longer sheds any germs
options.D: A healthcare worker who always wears proper personal protective equipment

explanation: Asymptomatic means no symptoms! They carry the germ around and feel totally fine, which is why infection control can be tricky. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h2)

question: What is a major challenge for injection safety in resource-limited settings like Nigeria?

options.A: An excessive surplus of modern safety-engineered syringes
options.B: Supply chain disruptions and shortages of safety devices
options.C: Complete lack of any national health guidelines or policies
options.D: Patients refusing to accept any injections from trained nurses

explanation: When clinics face stockouts of safety gear and syringes, it makes ideal infection control a tough daily battle for nurses. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h8)

question: Virginia Henderson is famous for giving us a clear checklist of fundamental human needs. How many are there on her list?
explanation: It's 14! Henderson outlined fourteen basic human needs that help us figure out exactly what kind of care our patients require. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T6#GNS112_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which mental health sign in degenerative brain disorders do families often mistake for sheer laziness?

options.A: Psychosis
options.B: Apathy
options.C: Delirium
options.D: Anxiety

explanation: You're doing great! Apathy means a deep lack of drive and emotion. Loved ones sometimes misunderstand this symptom as a patient just not trying hard enough. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h3)

question: Which of these is a key part of doing a full, holistic nursing assessment?

options.A: Exploring the patient's home support systems and cultural beliefs
options.B: Avoiding questions about mental health to prevent upsetting them
options.C: Rushing the patient to finish answering interview questions quickly
options.D: Focusing exclusively on laboratory values and bedside monitors

explanation: Awesome! Holistic assessments intentionally gather data on social, cultural, and emotional factors right alongside physical signs. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T2#GNS123_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the main difference between meningitis and encephalitis?

options.A: Encephalitis is always caused by fungi, while meningitis is always caused by bacteria.
options.B: Meningitis causes personality changes, while encephalitis only causes stiff joints.
options.C: Meningitis affects the spinal cord exclusively, while encephalitis affects only the skull.
options.D: Encephalitis involves inflammation of the brain tissue itself, while meningitis affects the protective membranes around it.

explanation: Meningitis targets the 'meninges' (the covering layers), while encephalitis targets the actual 'encephalon' (the brain tissue itself). Simple and easy to remember! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h3)

question: Which vaccine is routinely given during pregnancy to protect the newborn from a deadly infection?

options.A: Tetanus toxoid
options.B: Measles vaccine
options.C: Bacille Calmette-Guérin
options.D: Hepatitis A vaccine

explanation: Spot on! Tetanus toxoid is given to expectant mothers to protect their babies from neonatal tetanus. Great memory! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h3)

question: What exactly is Sheehan's syndrome?

options.A: Immune system attack on the adrenal glands brought on by stress
options.B: Death of pituitary tissue due to severe blood loss right after childbirth
options.C: A benign tumor causing sudden vision loss in older men
options.D: A genetic inability to make antidiuretic hormone after bumping your head

explanation: During delivery, a massive hemorrhage can drop blood pressure so low that the hardworking pituitary gland is starved of blood and oxygen, leading to tissue death (necrosis). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which foetal blood shunt connects the pulmonary artery straight to the descending aorta?

options.A: Ductus venosus
options.B: Ductus arteriosus
options.C: Umbilical vein
options.D: Foramen ovale

explanation: Great job! The ductus arteriosus safely redirects blood away from the baby's unventilated lungs directly into the aorta. Foetal circulation is fascinating once you get the hang of it! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h5)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse when patients want to use complementary or alternative therapies?

options.A: Forbidding patients from using any therapy not written in the doctor's orders
options.B: Personally performing massage and aromatherapy for every single patient
options.C: Ensuring safe use, providing education, and supporting patient preferences
options.D: Selling herbal supplements to patients to help fund the hospital ward

explanation: Well done! Nurses act as educators and safety advocates, helping patients safely blend alternative methods with their standard medical care. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T2#GNS123_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the name of the thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall that pumps blood?

options.A: Myocardium
options.B: Epicardium
options.C: Pericardium
options.D: Endocardium

explanation: The myocardium is the muscular middle layer of the heart that does the hard work of contracting and pumping blood to the body! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h1)

question: What electrolyte abnormality is a key feature of Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: High potassium
options.B: Low phosphate
options.C: High calcium
options.D: Low sodium

explanation: When massive numbers of cancer cells burst open, they flood the bloodstream with intracellular potassium, causing hyperkalemia. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which common side effect is frequently associated with the use of ACE inhibitors in cardiac patients?

options.A: A persistent dry cough
options.B: Severe hair loss
options.C: Uncontrollable tremors
options.D: Yellowing of the skin

explanation: ACE inhibitors cause a buildup of bradykinin in the lungs, which often triggers an irritating, non-productive dry cough in many patients. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h3)

question: What do we call painful swallowing caused by sores or irritation in the food pipe?

options.A: Dysphagia
options.B: Odynophagia
options.C: Regurgitation
options.D: Aspiration

explanation: Odynophagia is just the medical term for pain when you swallow. It usually happens when the lining is inflamed or has active sores. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T5#GNS213_U3_T5_h3)

question: A patient with an incomplete abortion has stable vital signs and no signs of severe infection. Which procedure is best for clearing her uterus?

options.A: Immediate total abdominal hysterectomy
options.B: Exploratory laparotomy with bowel resection
options.C: Intravenous broad-spectrum chemotherapy
options.D: Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA)

explanation: Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) is a quick, safe, and gentle method to clear out the remaining tissue in uncomplicated cases without needing heavy surgery. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T026#GNS226_U5_T026_h7)

question: What is the correct speed (rate) for giving breaths during neonatal positive pressure ventilation (PPV)?

options.A: 20 to 30 breaths per minute
options.B: 40 to 60 breaths per minute
options.C: 10 to 15 breaths per minute
options.D: 80 to 100 breaths per minute

explanation: When assisting a baby's breathing, aim for a steady, rhythmic pace of 40 to 60 breaths per minute to match a healthy newborn. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h4)

question: Why would a doctor choose skeletal traction over skin traction for a broken femur?

options.A: It requires no special monitoring by nursing staff
options.B: It completely eliminates the risk of infection
options.C: It allows much heavier weights to be used safely
options.D: It permits the patient to walk around the ward freely

explanation: Spot on! Because the pull goes straight to the bone, skeletal traction can handle the heavy weights needed to realign a big bone like the femur without tearing the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why is a case manager so important when a patient is getting ready to leave the hospital?

options.A: They prescribe the final discharge medications
options.B: They coordinate all services needed for a safe transition home
options.C: They perform the surgical follow-up check
options.D: They pay for the patient's hospital bills out of pocket

explanation: Case managers tie all the loose ends together—like equipment and home care visits—so the patient goes home smoothly without any gaps in care. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T7#GNS321_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the main role of the critical care nurse when family and medical teams disagree on life support choices?

options.A: Acting as a patient advocate to uphold their wishes and values
options.B: Directing the family members to leave the unit during discussions
options.C: Making the final legal decision on behalf of the medical team
options.D: Consulting hospital finance departments about treatment costs

explanation: Nurses stand up for the patient's voice, making sure their values and known preferences guide tough care choices. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T5#GNS321_U2_T5_h9)

question: What is the main goal of secondary prevention in healthcare?

options.A: Providing emergency surgery for severe trauma victims
options.B: Managing end-stage organ failure with palliative care
options.C: Early detection and prompt intervention for mild problems
options.D: Preventing a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person

explanation: Secondary prevention catches conditions early when they are easiest to treat and manage successfully. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T26#GNS312_U1_T26_h7)

question: Why are vasodilators frequently used in managing severe heart complications?

options.A: They widen blood vessels to reduce the resistance the heart must fight against
options.B: They make the heart beat at maximum speed instantly
options.C: They thicken the blood to raise blood pressure
options.D: They make blood clot much faster

explanation: Imagine trying to push water through a pinched garden hose vs. a wide-open pipe. Vasodilators open up the blood vessels, making it much easier for a tired heart to push blood forward! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of a living will?

options.A: To grant full medical licensing authority to a trusted family member
options.B: To distribute financial property and land ownership after death
options.C: To name a lawyer who will handle hospital bills and insurance claims
options.D: To outline specific medical treatments a person wants or refuses if terminally ill

explanation: A living will acts as the patient's voice on paper, stating their healthcare choices before they are too sick to speak. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you should do the moment an AED arrives?

options.A: Turn on the AED power
options.B: Check the patient for a carotid pulse
options.C: Deliver a manual shock immediately
options.D: Apply the adhesive pads to the chest

explanation: Just flip the power switch! The machine will start talking to you and guide you through every single step, making it super easy to follow. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T7#GNS321_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why is it important to ask if a patient has ever had surgery on their neck?

options.A: It can damage the thyroid or parathyroid glands
options.B: It stops the pancreas from producing insulin
options.C: It leads to chronic respiratory infections
options.D: It always causes permanent high blood pressure

explanation: Spot on! Because the thyroid and parathyroid glands live right in the neck, past surgeries there can sometimes accidentally disrupt hormone control. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a major environmental hazard in hospital corridors?

options.A: Soft carpeted flooring
options.B: Too many bright windows
options.C: Clutter and blocked pathways
options.D: Excessive room ventilation

explanation: Leaving equipment or boxes in hospital hallways creates clear tripping hazards for staff, visitors, and vulnerable patients. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is a known negative consequence of prolonged bed rest in older adults?

options.A: Immediate increase in bone mineral density
options.B: Rapid muscle atrophy and weakness
options.C: Complete elimination of fall risks
options.D: Enhanced joint cartilage regeneration

explanation: Inactivity quickly leads to muscle deconditioning, making it much harder for an older adult to regain mobility. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T24#GNS222_U1_T24_h7)

question: Why is it so crucial that a patient stays completely still during a spine CT scan?

options.A: Sudden movement triggers an emergency shutdown of the X-ray tube
options.B: Patient motion alters the chemical makeup of the radioactive dye
options.C: Body movement creates motion artifact that blurs the images and impairs diagnosis
options.D: Moving too fast can damage the sensitive internal rotating glass detectors

explanation: Even a tiny wiggle can blur the images (we call this 'motion artifact'), making it hard for the doctor to spot a fracture or issue. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical result of a major homeostatic breakdown?

options.A: Uncontrolled blood sugar spikes
options.B: Dangerous shifts in blood pH
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Balanced electrolyte levels in the blood

explanation: You got it! Balanced electrolytes mean homeostasis is winning and doing its job, not that it has broken down. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T7#GNS123_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which of the following is a primary way the community environment influences health?

options.A: Replacing the need for individual personal hygiene
options.B: Providing access to safe water, markets, and local clinics
options.C: Ensuring every citizen has a high-paying professional job
options.D: Eliminating all infectious diseases from the environment

explanation: Basic community infrastructure like clean water and nearby health clinics directly dictates physical well-being. [learn more](GNS112_U2_T4#GNS112_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is a major benefit of connecting family caregivers to local support groups?

options.A: It helps reduce caregiver burnout by sharing coping strategies and emotional support.
options.B: It provides free prescription medications directly to the household.
options.C: It completely cures the neurodegenerative disease process in the patient.
options.D: It eliminates the need for professional physical and occupational therapy.

explanation: Looking after someone with a chronic illness is tough work. Support groups give families a safe space to vent, share tips, and remember they are not alone in the journey. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h8)

question: Why should you give extra time when doing a mental assessment on an older adult?

options.A: Rushing can cause anxiety and lead to inaccurate assessment results
options.B: Older adults legally require thirty minutes per interview question
options.C: It gives the nurse time to complete paperwork during the session
options.D: Slowing down prevents the patient from hearing the questions

explanation: Thinking takes a little longer with age, so patience helps you get accurate answers and keeps the patient calm. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T3#GNS321_U3_T3_h7)

question: A patient with high blood pressure stops taking their antihypertensive drugs because they feel fine. What is the most likely outcome of this action?

options.A: The body permanently adjusts and cures the hypertension naturally
options.B: The liver will start producing its own natural blood pressure medicine
options.C: Blood pressure will stay normal as long as the patient eats well
options.D: The patient remains at high risk for silent organ damage and stroke

explanation: Hypertension is a chronic condition managed, not cured, by medications. Stopping treatment causes blood pressure to rise again, silently damaging vital organs like the heart and brain. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h2)

question: A client with an inherited degenerative disorder shows early muscle weakness and clumsy coordination. What should you do first?

options.A: Prepare the client for emergency surgery to repair the damaged genes
options.B: Document the findings, report the progression to the healthcare team, and assess safety needs
options.C: Tell the family that these mild symptoms will completely disappear within a week
options.D: Advise the client to stop all physical movement immediately to prevent further weakness

explanation: Spotting these changes early and planning for safety helps protect the client from falls as their motor skills decline. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T15#GNS222_U4_T15_h2)

question: As a nurse, why shouldn't you focus *only* on physical symptoms when caring for a client's reproductive health?

options.A: Because physical symptoms are rarely accurate indicators of reproductive disease
options.B: Because reproductive health includes mental, social, and bodily autonomy aspects
options.C: Because hospital policies strictly prohibit treating only physical complaints
options.D: Because laboratory tests cannot detect most reproductive system infections

explanation: You are caring for a human being, not just a body! Since reproductive health covers mental and social wellness too, great nurses look at the big picture. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T3#GNS216_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why are our eyes so dependent on rod cells when we are trying to see in the dark?

options.A: Rods block out distracting light rays in dark rooms
options.B: Rods are located only in the front part of the cornea
options.C: Rods are extremely sensitive to low levels of light
options.D: Rods produce the pigments needed to see bright colors at night

explanation: Rods don't do color very well, but they are night-vision champions! They only need a tiny glimmer of light to help us spot shapes and shadows in the dark. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of a needle holder during wound closure?

options.A: To clamp bleeding blood vessels in the subcutaneous fat
options.B: To pull back skin edges for a better view of the muscle
options.C: To cut excess suture thread after the knot is tied
options.D: To firmly grip the needle and drive it through tissue safely

explanation: Needle holders provide a strong, stable grip so the surgeon can guide the needle through tough layers without slipping. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T9#GNS123_U5_T9_h7)

question: Why should nurses avoid using vague words like 'normal' when charting physical assessments?

options.A: It violates patient privacy laws to write short descriptive sentences
options.B: Patients have a legal right to erase that word from their records
options.C: Hospital computers will automatically reject entries containing that word
options.D: Different healthcare workers can interpret vague words in different ways

explanation: Correct! Using clear, descriptive details ensures every nurse or doctor reading the chart has the exact same picture of the patient's condition. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h7)

question: How do bureaucratic silos hurt community health networks?

options.A: They eliminate all communication costs between health facilities
options.B: They prevent organizations from sharing data and coordinating their community interventions effectively
options.C: They automatically increase the number of trained midwives in rural areas
options.D: They force government ministries to merge with private pharmaceutical companies

explanation: Spot on! When agencies work in separate bubbles, resources get wasted and important gaps pop up in patient care. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T019#GNS226_U5_T019_h7)

question: What does the letter 'T' stand for in the GATHER counselling model?

options.A: Trust
options.B: Test
options.C: Tell
options.D: Touch

explanation: In GATHER, 'Tell' refers to sharing relevant and balanced information about available contraceptive methods with the client. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T022#GNS226_U6_T022_h3)

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient expresses deep fear that their cancer will return?

options.A: Change the subject immediately to something more positive
options.B: Acknowledge their feelings and provide a safe space to talk
options.C: Assure them with certainty that the cancer will never come back
options.D: Tell them not to worry because worrying brings the cancer back

explanation: Empathy first! Validating their fears and being there to listen helps them process heavy emotions instead of bottling them up. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: Why is family counseling so valuable when coping with a progressive illness?

options.A: It forces family members to move into the same household
options.B: It eliminates all future disagreements about financial matters
options.C: It helps resolve conflicts and adjust roles regarding care responsibilities
options.D: It proves which family member caused the inherited genetic mutation

explanation: As illnesses progress, family roles shift. Counseling gives everyone a safe space to talk openly and share the care burden smoothly. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T18#GNS222_U4_T18_h5)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to understand a patient's cultural background regarding death and grief?

options.A: Grief customs and expressions vary greatly across different cultures
options.B: Cultural practices are the only factor that influences healing
options.C: All cultures follow the exact same five stages of grief
options.D: Hospital policy requires every patient to have a religious burial

explanation: Culture dictates how people mourn, and understanding this helps nurses provide respectful, personalized support. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T8#GNS321_U4_T8_h7)

question: What is the best position for a patient during a thoracocentesis?

options.A: Lying flat on their stomach with the head turned to the side
options.B: Lying flat on their back with arms straight down
options.C: Sitting upright and leaning forward over a bedside table
options.D: Standing upright against a rigid wall with eyes closed

explanation: This posture widens the spaces between the ribs, making it safer and easier to insert the needle. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T17#GNS221_U2_T17_h3)

question: Why is it important to know if a seizure was 'provoked' by a temporary issue rather than epilepsy?

options.A: Epilepsy is strictly a pediatric condition that resolves after puberty
options.B: Provoked seizures never involve loss of consciousness
options.C: Provoked seizures are caused by temporary triggers and may not need lifelong drugs
options.D: Epilepsy can only be diagnosed if the patient has had at least ten seizures

explanation: Spot on! If a seizure is caused by something fixable like low sodium or a high fever, treating the root cause stops the seizures without needing long-term medication. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h4)

question: Which of the following is an immediate complication of FGM?

options.A: Severe bleeding and shock
options.B: Chronic kidney failure
options.C: Gestational diabetes
options.D: High blood pressure

explanation: The immediate trauma of cutting sensitive tissue often leads to heavy bleeding and surgical shock. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T5#GNS312_U1_T5_h3)

question: What do we call the breathing difficulty that gets worse when a patient lies flat?

options.A: Sudden breathlessness that occurs only at noon
options.B: Inability to speak full sentences due to pain
options.C: Breathlessness that worsens when lying flat
options.D: Shortness of breath triggered by cold air

explanation: That's orthopnoea! Patients naturally prop themselves up with pillows to catch their breath. You will see this often in heart failure cases. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T13#GNS123_U3_T13_h3)
